facts.text: Many drivers use phone navigation to follow a route through unfamiliar towns.
Families still keep a spare tire or repair kit for roadside emergencies.
A school bus stops along residential streets to collect children each weekday morning.
Parents wait in a line of cars outside the school at dismissal time.
Some teenagers practice for a driving test with a parent in the passenger seat.
A driver checks tire pressure before a long highway trip.
Many gas stations offer pumps where customers pay with a card.
Some motorists stop at a convenience store attached to a fuel station.
Electric cars are increasingly visible on town streets and highways.
An electric car owner may plan a longer journey around available charging stations.
Public charging stations appear at some shopping centers and parking lots.
Drivers of older vehicles still visit garages for oil changes and routine repairs.
A family may choose a used vehicle because a new one costs too much.
Children ride bicycles along neighborhood streets and shared paths.
Some cyclists wear reflective clothing when riding after dark.
A town may mark bicycle lanes along busier streets.
Pedestrians use marked crosswalks near schools and shopping streets.
A commuter may share a ride with a coworker to save on fuel.
Residents in small towns often need a car for errands beyond the town center.
Some intercity bus routes connect smaller communities with regional cities.
Passenger trains serve certain towns, but many communities have no nearby station.
During 2020, some families cancel road trips because of travel restrictions and health concerns.
During 2020, many commuters drive less while working from home.
During 2021, some car buyers encounter limited dealer inventory.
During 2022, high gasoline prices prompt drivers to combine errands into fewer trips.
Some newer cars warn drivers when they drift out of a marked lane.
A driver may use a dashboard camera to record a journey.
A family packs snacks and water before setting out on a long road trip.
